title: Geometry-Aware Optimal Transport: Fast Intrinsic Dimension and Wasserstein Distance Estimation
claim: Our estimator matches the accuracy of the expensive baseline while running orders of magnitude faster than it.
layout: 2 panels, left grouped bars plus right log-scale time bars, shared legend below
description: Two bar-chart panels sharing one legend along the bottom. The large left panel shows estimated dimension for three datasets: Mixture (Uniform), Mixture (Gaussian) and Pure Gaussian. Each dataset has six hatched, colored bars: CorrInt, Discrete W1, MLE, Semi-Discrete W1 (ours), TwoNN and lPCA. Error bars sit on top of the bars. A dashed horizontal line labeled 'True Dim' marks 10. Discrete W1 and the semi-discrete method sit near the line on the mixtures, while the other estimators fall far below it. The narrow right panel shows mean runtime on a log scale. Discrete W1 takes 10.50s and the semi-discrete method takes 0.01s. Each bar is annotated with a rotated time label. The eye goes first to the tall orange bars and the dashed line.
caption: Intrinsic Dimension Estimation Benchmark. Comparison of our Semi-Discrete $W_1$ estimator against the Discrete $W_1$ baseline and standard geometric estimators. The dashed line represents the ground truth effective dimension $\dint = 10$. Our estimator matches the robustness of discrete OT on mixtures but runs orders of magnitude faster ($<0.1$s vs $\sim 10$s).
abstract: Solving large scale Optimal Transport (OT) in machine learning typically relies on sampling measures to obtain a tractable discrete problem. While the discrete solver's accuracy is controllable, the rate of convergence of the discretization error is governed by the intrinsic dimension of our data. Therefore, the true bottleneck is the knowledge and control of the sampling error. In this work, we tackle this issue by introducing novel estimators for both sampling error and intrinsic dimension. The key finding is a simple, tuning-free estimator of $\text{OT}_c(Ï, \hatÏ)$ that utilizes the semi-dual OT functional and, remarkably, requires no OT solver. Furthermore, we derive a fast intrinsic dimension estimator from the multi-scale decay of our sampling error estimator. This framework unlocks significant computational and statistical advantages in practice, enabling us to (i) quantify the convergence rate of the discretization error, (ii) calibrate the entropic regularization of Sinkhorn divergences to the data's intrinsic geometry, and (iii) introduce a novel, intrinsic-dimension-based Richardson extrapolation estimator that strongly debiases Wasserstein distance estimation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our geometry-aware pipeline effectively mitigates the discretization error bottleneck while maintaining computational efficiency.
